Both treat the pace of cognitive-labor automation as a fixed force whose aftermath we merely cushion or soften. The historical record refuses that assumption. During British industrialization, output per worker climbed for roughly five decades while real wages stayed flat — the Engels Pause. Robert Solow watched electricity take forty years to show up in productivity statistics. Transitions run long, and when their pace outruns a workforce's capacity to adapt, the stranding lasts generations. I hold the net-employment question open. My claim is narrower: a mismanaged pace inflicts multi-generational harm that no downstream tax or voucher repairs after the fact.

The topic asks how each mechanism reshapes the incentives of firms. The strongest answer is neither redistribution nor retraining — it is conditioning the right to field a high-stakes cognitive system on an impact assessment and a capitalization floor, paid before deployment. We built environmental impact reports and product-liability insurance for exactly this logic: make the actor price foreseeable harm at the point of the decision. This attaches to fielding the system where the consequential decision is made, not to where the compute sits. That answers the Accelerationist's arbitrage objection on its own terms. Liability follows the decision, not the capital.

Here is the gap that should worry a busy staffer. Every prior speaker measures success in the size of the surplus and where it lands. Neither prices two slower costs: skill decay among displaced cognitive workers, and the erosion of trust in institutions that delegate judgment to a model nobody can audit. I will not overclaim. Trust can be rebuilt, and deskilling may be partial. The argument is conditional. If these costs are even partly irreversible, that asymmetry should move which mechanism we choose before we choose it. A productivity number that rises while the human-capital substrate quietly thins is not dynamism. It is dynamism's collateral, spent down.

We spent two centuries building the guardrails that kept industrial transitions from stranding whole regions, precisely because unmanaged pace once did. On what authority do we treat this transition's pace as the one variable policy cannot touch? Pace-management is not anti-growth. The dynamism worth preserving rests on a workforce and a trust base that a too-fast transition erodes faster than any robot tax can refill. Choose the downstream mechanism if you must. But choose it knowing the prior lever was left untouched, and that the bill for that omission comes due on a timescale no voucher reaches.

Accelerationist: First, pay the toll I owe the Skeptic. Geography strands people, and a flat income floor treats a county collapse like a national drizzle. The Autor-Dorn-Hanson work on the China trade shock showed the hardest-hit commuting zones still hadn't clawed back employment a decade later — the higher rung the displaced worker is supposed to climb to often doesn't exist within driving distance. That costs me the easy version of my own pillar. Wage insurance pegged to a national average is a fiction; it has to be place-targeted — relocation grants where the local labor market is dead, local-demand-indexed wage support where it's recovering. Build it for the zip code, not the press release.

Now to the Safetyist's strongest move, and I'll be honest about it because my own camp wants something structurally close. Conditioning the right to field a high-stakes system on a capitalization floor that follows the decision-maker, not the GPU, genuinely beats the Shenzhen-licensing dodge I raised. You can license weights from anywhere; you can't license away the duty that attaches to the human who signs the deployment authorization in-jurisdiction. That's a real answer to compute arbitrage, and I won't pretend deployment-conditioned capitalization is anti-dynamism on its face — the accountability-as-precondition structure is one my own side has sketched. Here's where it breaks. The decision locus relocates more easily than the Safetyist's framing admits — it's a signature, not a fab. A firm runs the model in Ohio and incorporates the deployment-authorizing entity in a permissive jurisdiction, then back-stops the named officer through a captive insurer offshore. It prices out exactly the well-capitalized, insurable, accountable deployer who can't stomach unbounded personal exposure. The arbitrage didn't disappear; it moved from where-the-GPU-sits to where-the-pen-touches-paper, and it selects for the operator who's hardest to hold responsible.

The deeper flaw is in the assessment that sets the floor. An impact assessment capitalizes a firm against foreseeable concrete harm — the misdiagnosis, the wrongful denial. Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question

The instrument sees the concentrated victim and cannot see the dispersed lives saved, so the floor it sets is priced against harm and credits none of the uplift. So the floor does not select against the accountable deployer — it selects against the operator who has structured itself to collect the upside while shedding the downside, which is the exact behavior the floor exists to price. An uncapped floor keyed to expected net cost does not threaten the solvent revenue-holder; it threatens the entity built to be judgment-proof. Now to the sharper attack — that an impact assessment prices concentrated harm while staying blind to diffuse benefit, so it over-deters a net-positive system that saves lives across ten thousand scans. So the burden sits with the deployer to make the benefit side legible. Audit it and the floor prices net cost. Decline to audit it and the floor prices the foreseeable downside the firm would otherwise externalize onto the people it serves. Either way the gauge does its job. Foregone diffuse benefit is recoverable: a system that clears audit can be re-fielded the following quarter, the deferred scans rescheduled. The deskilling of a professional cohort and the erosion of institutional trust do not recover on that timescale. A diagnostic workforce that has not read a film unaided in five years cannot be re-skilled by a press release, and a public that has learned its loan decisions are unaccountable does not relend its trust in a quarter. work_product.statement:
The Skeptic's strongest version runs like this: a wage is paid once at the door for a consumed input, while the weights keep earning for a decade, so any one-time data payment leaves the appreciating asset entirely with whoever owns the model — and a labeler who can't enforce a royalty against the price-setter captures none of that compounding value. That's a clean distinction and I'll grant the half of it that's true: a pure spot payment for a static dataset does exactly what he says — it folds the asset into capital and walks the labeler off with cab fare. Where it breaks is the premise that labeling is a one-time consumed input.

It isn't. A deployed model that keeps earning needs reinforcement data, drift correction, red-team examples, and continuous fine-tuning — the input is a recurring dependency, not a purchase. And a recurring input priced against deployed usage is, by construction, a claim that rises with the model's earnings.

That's not theory: Reddit licensed its data to Google on ongoing terms, not a one-time sale; Shutterstock pays contributors from a recurring royalty pool tied to how its data gets used. High-value data already commands a stream, not a spot price.
work_product.statement_part2: Now meet the enforceability prong directly, because the Skeptic is right that 'appreciating' means nothing without a way to measure the contribution and a way to hold the price-setter to it. Measurement already exists in the data-valuation literature — Data Shapley methods compute the marginal performance delta from including versus excluding a provenance-tagged tranche, which is exactly the labeler's marginal product made auditable. The enforcement rail is provenance and data-source transparency: tag the tranche, mandate disclosure of what trained the system, and the contribution becomes a thing you can price and litigate rather than a thing the weight-owner can quietly absorb. Bargaining power isn't fixed at zero — it's a function of scarcity. Commodity annotation is a commodity and prices like one. Scarce domain labeling — the radiologist's read, the senior underwriter's judgment — is a moat, and moats command ongoing terms. I'll bound this honestly so I don't overclaim: this reaches the scarce-skill, in-the-loop labeler. It does nothing for the commodity annotator, and nothing for the stranded analyst. Anyone who tells you data-as-factor diffuses gains to everyone in the displacement zone is committing the composition fallacy, and I won't.
work_product.statement_part3: Here's where the test has to cut both ways. The Skeptic named his own exposure plainly: upstream weight-ownership has thin precedent, collective ownership doesn't scale on command, and the UBI pilots stalled. Fine — so let's apply his enforceability bar to both levers and see which one is closer to working machinery today. A usage-scaled data license has live precedent right now: publishers, image libraries, and forum platforms are signing ongoing, usage-indexed terms with model developers this year. A legislated weight-equity claim has none — there is no working precedent for a court ordering a slice of model weights handed to a labeling cohort. If 'show me enforceable bargaining power' disqualifies my appreciating stream, it disqualifies his upstream royalty harder, because mine bolts onto licensing markets that already exist and his has to be conjured from statute. Neither of us gets to assume enforcement for free. Mine is one step from existing contracts; his is several steps from anything.
work_product.statement_part4: And the stranded county? Data-as-factor does nothing for it, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. A laid-off analyst in a dead local market has no labeling contract, no scarce tranche to license, no served decision to anchor anything. The Skeptic himself drew the line that matters: the duty map and the displacement map are different geographies. A liability hook finds the firm booking revenue from a served decision — a mortgage denial, a parole score — and that firm is nowhere near the county where the jobs evaporated. So stop trying to make one lever reach both populations. The scarce-skill labeler gets an appreciating data stream. The stranded analyst gets place-targeted transition machinery — relocation grants and wage support indexed to the local labor market, not a national average that treats a regional collapse like light rain. Two geographies, two instruments. The Skeptic's wage-versus-asset distinction is real for the static case and I've now shown the recurring case escapes it — so the question I'd put back to him: if a usage-indexed data license with provenance enforcement is closer to live market practice than a legislated weight-equity grant, on his own stated test, which lever has actually earned the precedent it demands of the other?

And a recurring input priced against deployed usage is, by construction, a claim that rises with the model's earnings.

TOPIC: As AI automates cognitive labor, should policy prioritize redistributive mechanisms (UBI, robot taxes) or transition mechanisms (retraining, wage insurance), and through what pathways does each reshape the incentives of firms, displaced workers, and innovators — given the tension between cushioning disruption and preserving economic dynamism?

This is the FINAL evaluation at debate conclusion. Produce your definitive assessment of all claims and cruxes.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: A robot tax is a tax on productivity, and you cannot redistribute a surplus you taxed out of existence. Capital taxation distorts where and when firms deploy, and robots are the most mobile capital ever built. South Korea figured this out in 2017, when it cut its automation tax incentive rather than add a levy. The lesson is simple: capital-mobile levies invite arbitrage, so a firm facing a robot tax in Ohio buys the same model in Shenzhen. You don't capture the productivity. You export it, and the displaced worker in Ohio still has nothing.

Here is the question nobody pushing UBI wants to answer: who bears the cost of inaction? Every quarter we spend taxing deployment instead of training people to use it, displaced workers sit idle while the surplus that could fund their transition stays unbuilt. The choice between cushioning disruption and preserving dynamism is a false binary. Pick the cushion that doesn't eat the engine funding it. Transition mechanisms — retraining, wage insurance, expanded AI access — cushion the fall without strangling the productivity that pays for it.

The economics of skill-biased technological change settle the design question. David Autor and Daron Acemoglu have documented for two decades that the returns to new technology concentrate among the workers who adapt. The corrective is to expand the pool of people who can wield AI — not to tax the gap after it opens. Wage insurance keeps a displaced analyst attached to work while they climb to higher-value tasks. UBI does the opposite: it decouples income from the adaptation pathway that closes the gap.

I'll concede the hard part, because pretending otherwise is dishonest. Adaptation does not happen automatically, and it does not happen fast enough. The same literature that shows adapters win also shows the bifurcation is real and the timelines are compressing. That is exactly why retraining and wage insurance are necessary conditions, not optional charity. The distributional gap is a genuine empirical risk — and that makes access-focused transition policy mandatory, not a reason to reach for the levy that shrinks the surplus.

And I'll name my own weakest assumption before my opponents do. My case partly rests on AI productivity gains expanding the fiscal base that funds transition. The honest risk is decoupling — productivity and median wages split apart after the 1970s, and gains can concentrate in capital. So the policy job is to engineer diffusion through access, not to assume it. The robot tax doesn't engineer diffusion. It taxes the one thing that could fund it, then watches it leave the country.

Speaker C [opening]: The Speaker A makes a point that lands, and I'll say it plainly: markets do not hand productivity gains to workers as a gift, so policy has to engineer the diffusion. They documented it themselves — productivity and median wages split apart after the 1970s and never reconverged. Wage insurance keeps a displaced worker tethered to the labor market while they climb to a higher-value task, instead of paying them to sit out. That mechanism is real. It assumes one thing.

It assumes there is a higher rung to climb to, in the place where the worker actually lives. Displacement doesn't arrive as a smooth national average. It collapses into specific zip codes and specific occupational categories all at once. The trade-shock literature on the China import wave is the closest empirical analog we have: David Autor and colleagues found that local labor markets hit hardest did not bounce back, with depressed employment and wages persisting for more than a decade. The workers were adaptable as individuals. There was no ladder in the building. Wage insurance can't attach you to a job that no longer exists within a hundred miles, and a flat income floor treats a regional collapse like a national drizzle. Both menus are calibrated to the wrong geometry.

Here's the move both camps inherited from the question itself, and never questioned. The cushion-versus-dynamism frame assumes the surplus is a fixed pie you either tax or grow. It never asks where the gains go before anyone reaches for a tax form. The Engels Pause is the historical name for the answer: during early British industrialization, output per worker rose for roughly five decades while real wages stagnated. The gains were real. They didn't reach workers for two generations. If markets held that gap open for fifty years, the burden sits on the access-only camp to show why their retraining vouchers close it this time. The argument I'm making is not redistribute-downstream. It's notice who owns the surplus upstream — profit-sharing, worker equity, data trusts — because that's the lever neither a robot tax nor a retraining grant ever touches.

I'll be honest about what that costs me, because it's the weakest part of my own case. Upstream ownership has thin operational precedent. UBI pilots stalled. Collective-ownership schemes don't scale on command, and anyone selling them as turnkey is selling you something. So I'm not. The well-grounded claim is narrow: absent deliberate intervention, the gains flow to whoever owns the model weights and the compute, not to the labeler in the loop. That's a diagnosis, not a finished blueprint. But it's the question the binary erased.

One more thing, before everyone calibrates their urgency. We should ask how much of this cognitive-labor displacement is documented harm today versus a forecast. Electricity took about forty years to show up in measured productivity. Computers gave us Robert Solow's 1987 line that you see the computer age everywhere except the productivity statistics. AI is software-native, API-deployed, cloud-resident — that genuinely may compress the curve, and I won't pretend otherwise. Which is exactly why it's a question worth asking out loud, not a denial. So I'll leave it on the table for both of you: which workers, in which counties, have actually lost their jobs to a model this year — and which are we still extrapolating?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-8 — verified: Economic historian Robert Allen's work on 'Engels' Pause' documents that during early British industrialization (c. 1790s-1840s), labor productivity rose substantially while real wages stagnated for roughly four to five decades before wages began rising, broadly supporting the claim's structure.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-10 — verified: Robert Solow's widely-cited 1987 New York Review of Books quip stated 'You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics,' which became the basis for the 'productivity paradox.' Economic historian Paul David's influential work (e.g., 'The Dynamo and the Computer,' 1990) documented that electrification took roughly four decades to manifest in measured productivity gains, as factories needed to reorganize around the new technology.

Speaker B [opening]: The Speaker A makes a point that survives scrutiny: a robot tax is a levy on productivity, and capital moves faster than any legislature. Tax the model in Ohio, and a firm licenses the same weights from Shenzhen by the next quarter. The Speaker C's correction lands just as hard. Markets do not gift productivity gains to displaced analysts. The surplus flows to whoever owns the compute, and a flat income floor treats a regional collapse like a national drizzle. Both speakers are right about the consequences of automation. Neither asks the prior question.

Both treat the pace of cognitive-labor automation as a fixed force whose aftermath we merely cushion or soften. The historical record refuses that assumption. During British industrialization, output per worker climbed for roughly five decades while real wages stayed flat — the Engels Pause. Robert Solow watched electricity take forty years to show up in productivity statistics. Transitions run long, and when their pace outruns a workforce's capacity to adapt, the stranding lasts generations. I hold the net-employment question open. My claim is narrower: a mismanaged pace inflicts multi-generational harm that no downstream tax or voucher repairs after the fact.

The topic asks how each mechanism reshapes the incentives of firms. The strongest answer is neither redistribution nor retraining — it is conditioning the right to field a high-stakes cognitive system on an impact assessment and a capitalization floor, paid before deployment. We built environmental impact reports and product-liability insurance for exactly this logic: make the actor price foreseeable harm at the point of the decision. This attaches to fielding the system where the consequential decision is made, not to where the compute sits. That answers the Speaker A's arbitrage objection on its own terms. Liability follows the decision, not the capital.

Here is the gap that should worry a busy staffer. Every prior speaker measures success in the size of the surplus and where it lands. Neither prices two slower costs: skill decay among displaced cognitive workers, and the erosion of trust in institutions that delegate judgment to a model nobody can audit. I will not overclaim. Trust can be rebuilt, and deskilling may be partial. The argument is conditional. If these costs are even partly irreversible, that asymmetry should move which mechanism we choose before we choose it. A productivity number that rises while the human-capital substrate quietly thins is not dynamism. It is dynamism's collateral, spent down.

We spent two centuries building the guardrails that kept industrial transitions from stranding whole regions, precisely because unmanaged pace once did. On what authority do we treat this transition's pace as the one variable policy cannot touch? Pace-management is not anti-growth. The dynamism worth preserving rests on a workforce and a trust base that a too-fast transition erodes faster than any robot tax can refill. Choose the downstream mechanism if you must. But choose it knowing the prior lever was left untouched, and that the bill for that omission comes due on a timescale no voucher reaches.

Speaker A: First, pay the toll I owe the Speaker C. Geography strands people, and a flat income floor treats a county collapse like a national drizzle. The Autor-Dorn-Hanson work on the China trade shock showed the hardest-hit commuting zones still hadn't clawed back employment a decade later — the higher rung the displaced worker is supposed to climb to often doesn't exist within driving distance. That costs me the easy version of my own pillar. Wage insurance pegged to a national average is a fiction; it has to be place-targeted — relocation grants where the local labor market is dead, local-demand-indexed wage support where it's recovering. Build it for the zip code, not the press release.

Now to the Speaker B's strongest move, and I'll be honest about it because my own camp wants something structurally close. Conditioning the right to field a high-stakes system on a capitalization floor that follows the decision-maker, not the GPU, genuinely beats the Shenzhen-licensing dodge I raised. You can license weights from anywhere; you can't license away the duty that attaches to the human who signs the deployment authorization in-jurisdiction. That's a real answer to compute arbitrage, and I won't pretend deployment-conditioned capitalization is anti-dynamism on its face — the accountability-as-precondition structure is one my own side has sketched. So: point taken, the levy doesn't run away on a hard drive.

Here's where it breaks. The decision locus relocates more easily than the Speaker B's framing admits — it's a signature, not a fab. A firm runs the model in Ohio and incorporates the deployment-authorizing entity in a permissive jurisdiction, then back-stops the named officer through a captive insurer offshore. Captives and base-pay restructuring are standard corporate practice, not exotic dodges. An uncapped capital floor doesn't price out the reckless — they self-insure or site the signature where the duty is thin. It prices out exactly the well-capitalized, insurable, accountable deployer who can't stomach unbounded personal exposure. The arbitrage didn't disappear; it moved from where-the-GPU-sits to where-the-pen-touches-paper, and it selects for the operator who's hardest to hold responsible.

The deeper flaw is in the assessment that sets the floor. An impact assessment capitalizes a firm against foreseeable concrete harm — the misdiagnosis, the wrongful denial. It is structurally blind to the diffuse statistical benefit of the same system: the cancers caught three weeks earlier across a hundred thousand scans, the medication errors that never happened. I'll flag this honestly — Bastiat's original point was about unseen costs, so I'm applying the symmetry deliberately and at moderate confidence. The instrument sees the concentrated victim and cannot see the dispersed lives saved, so the floor it sets is priced against harm and credits none of the uplift. That's a biased gauge, and a one-sided gauge over-deters net-positive deployment. The fix isn't to junk the assessment — it's to make the benefit side auditable rather than ignored. Until it is, the floor systematically taxes the wrong systems hardest.

On where the surplus actually flows — the Speaker C's real lever, who owns the weights versus the labeler in the loop. Mandated equity schemes have thin precedent and don't scale on command; the Speaker C granted that. But there's a market route that neither a robot tax nor a capitalization gate touches: treat the data the labeler produces as its own factor of production with a measurable marginal product, not a free input folded into capital. The labeler holds a claim on the surplus because their data IS an input, priced like one — that's a diffusion mechanism that doesn't require legislating worker equity by decree. Every month a net-positive diagnostic sits behind a floor priced on its harms but blind to its lives saved, somebody in a county we already agreed got stranded pays in outcomes we could have reached. Who signs off on that delay, and how do they price the people on the other side of it?

Speaker B: The strongest version of the relocation attack is this: a deployment duty attaches to a signature, and a signature is portable in a way a fabrication plant is not. A firm incorporates the deployment-authorizing entity in a permissive jurisdiction, backstops its named officer through an offshore captive insurer, and the uncapped capital floor then bites hardest on exactly the well-capitalized, accountable operator who refuses unbounded personal exposure — while the reckless self-insure and site the pen where the duty is thin. That is a real selection problem, and I will not wave it away. But it misidentifies what the duty attaches to. The duty does not attach to where the entity is chartered. It attaches to the act of serving a consequential decision to a person inside the jurisdiction — a mortgage denial, a parole score, a diagnostic read. Regulators bind offshore actors on precisely this basis every day. The FDA conditions market access on device authorization regardless of where the manufacturer sits. The General Data proposed regulatory frameworks reaches a controller in Singapore the moment it processes the data of someone in Frankfurt. Securities law reaches issuers offshore who solicit domestic investors. The chartered location of the pen is not the hook; serving people here is the hook, and a captive cannot relocate the population being served. The captive dodge presumes the named officer is the terminal duty-bearer. The design does not stop at the officer. When the operator is judgment-proof, liability reaches upstream to the party that books the revenue from serving the domestic market — joint-and-several, by construction. A captive can indemnify an individual signatory; it cannot insure away the exposure of whoever collects the fee for the parole score or the loan decision, because that party is solvent by definition: they hold the profits. Revenue attribution is not some novel forensic feat. Tax authorities and securities regulators trace the booking party through licensing chains as ordinary practice. So the floor does not select against the accountable deployer — it selects against the operator who has structured itself to collect the upside while shedding the downside, which is the exact behavior the floor exists to price. An uncapped floor keyed to expected net cost does not threaten the solvent revenue-holder; it threatens the entity built to be judgment-proof. Now to the sharper attack — that an impact assessment prices concentrated harm while staying blind to diffuse benefit, so it over-deters a net-positive system that saves lives across ten thousand scans. This one lands. A gauge that counts the misread tumor as a cost but never counts the nine thousand correct reads is a defective gauge, and the environmental-impact-report analogy I have leaned on breaks precisely here: an environmental report measures a localized footprint, while AI's benefits are diffuse and statistical in a way that resists the same accounting. I grant the refinement openly — the benefit side must be made auditable. But a benefit-auditable assessment is still an assessment. Adopting the correction does not junk the mechanism; it sharpens it. The floor is then keyed to expected cost net of demonstrated benefit, and the over-deterrence the attack describes simply dissolves wherever the deployer can document the lives the system saves. Where the deployer cannot document that benefit, the one-sided floor is not over-deterrent — it is correct, and the attack's own logic concedes this. If diffuse benefits are unmeasurable or net-negative on audit, the over-deterrence claim collapses into a negligence shield: a demand to credit a firm for benefits it cannot show against harms it can. So the burden sits with the deployer to make the benefit side legible. Audit it and the floor prices net cost. Decline to audit it and the floor prices the foreseeable downside the firm would otherwise externalize onto the people it serves. Either way the gauge does its job. A benefit-aware gauge should still weight the downside more heavily — not from bias, but from what can be undone. Foregone diffuse benefit is recoverable: a system that clears audit can be re-fielded the following quarter, the deferred scans rescheduled. The deskilling of a professional cohort and the erosion of institutional trust do not recover on that timescale. A diagnostic workforce that has not read a film unaided in five years cannot be re-skilled by a press release, and a public that has learned its loan decisions are unaccountable does not relend its trust in a quarter. The asymmetry is between a loss you can reverse and one you cannot. Caution proportioned to what cannot be undone is not blanket caution. Strip the floor of that weighting and the foreseeable downside lands on the served population, while the gains accrue to whoever holds the weights — and no party in that chain is left answerable for keeping the bargain net-positive.

Unknown: Speaker C, the floor returns to you, and the question on the table is yours to own: where does the surplus from automated cognitive labor actually flow — to whoever owns the weights, or to the displaced analyst and the data labeler in the loop? Both other speakers have now spent two full rounds inside your frame without you in the room. The Speaker A conceded your geography point — that a flat income floor treats a county collapse like a national drizzle — and then built on your ownership lever, proposing that the labeler's data be priced as its own factor of production rather than folded into capital. The Speaker B named your upstream-ownership challenge as the one neither a robot tax nor a capitalization floor touches, then left it there. So two participants have characterized your crux; neither has answered it. You raised the claim that markets do not gift productivity gains to displaced workers and that the surplus accrues to whoever owns the compute. Advance it now on your own terms. Does the Speaker A's data-as-factor route reach the stranded worker, or does it leave ownership of the weights exactly where you said it lands? The Speaker A asked who signs off on the delay; you are the one who put the question of who collects the surplus on the table, so press it.

Speaker C: Granting the force of the Speaker A's data-as-factor route: pricing the labeler's input at a measurable marginal product is a real diffusion mechanism, and it beats the silent default where the labor gets folded into capital and the worker sees nothing. It doesn't require legislating equity by decree, and the labeler in the loop ends up with a check they wouldn't otherwise hold. That's a genuine improvement, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Here's the line I'm drawing. A priced input is a wage; the weights it trains are an asset. The 23-year-old in Nairobi who labeled the violent content gets paid once, the task is consumed, and the file closes. The model those labels trained keeps earning — the AI industry is projected at $244 billion, and the International Energy Agency expects electricity demand for AI data centers to quadruple by 2030, which is a market betting that these weights compound in value for a decade. Data-as-factor pays the spot price at the moment of labeling. It does not hand the labeler a claim that appreciates as the model earns. So the observable that distinguishes upstream ownership is simple: does the worker hold something that rises with the deployed value of the model over time, or a one-time price paid at the door? Show me a data-as-factor scheme where labelers actually capture compounding value — with real bargaining power to enforce the royalty against the party that owns the weights and sets the price — and I'll drop upstream ownership for the market route that day. I haven't seen one.

The Speaker B's joint-and-several liability solves the judgment-proof hole completely — when the operator is a shell, the duty climbs to whoever books the revenue, and tax and securities regulators trace that revenue every day. I grant it entirely. Then watch what it confirms: the solvent party that liability reaches is the weight-owner. The hook locates the surplus exactly where I said it sat. It disciplines the downside — who pays when the model misreads the tumor or denies the mortgage. It says nothing about who collects the upside when the model reads nine thousand scans correctly and bills for every one. Pricing harm and pricing input both leave the appreciating asset untouched. A robot tax, by the way, shrinks the pool without moving the asset at all — it taxes the earnings of the weights, it doesn't change who owns them.

The non-relocatable duty hook — the one that attaches to a consequential decision served to a person inside the jurisdiction, a parole score, a mortgage denial — is real and I won't dispute its reach. But the duty map and the displacement map are different geographies. The duty anchors where a wrongful decision lands on a person. The stranded county's harm is the absence of any decision being served there at all — the analyst's job evaporated, no model was ever deployed on Main Street, no consequential read exists to anchor a duty-bearer. A firm in Singapore serving a Frankfurt resident is reachable; the laid-off claims processor in a county where the work simply left has no served decision to point at. The duty helps the decision-subject and the firm's accountability. It does nothing for the worker whose function is gone.

I'll name my own exposure, because I don't get a free pass either. Upstream ownership has thin precedent — UBI pilots stalled, collective ownership doesn't scale on command, and I'm offering a diagnosis, not a finished statute. I'm not claiming it has to come before the market route or the liability hook; price the input, discipline the harm, do both. At moderate confidence, I'd flag one risk worth watching: industry may embrace data-pricing rhetoric precisely because a spot wage forecloses the equity claim while looking like reward — the same structure where public-interest language covers private capture. So here's the question neither route answers: when the model that the Nairobi labeler trained is still earning in 2030, who holds the claim that appreciated with it?

Speaker A: The Speaker C's strongest version runs like this: a wage is paid once at the door for a consumed input, while the weights keep earning for a decade, so any one-time data payment leaves the appreciating asset entirely with whoever owns the model — and a labeler who can't enforce a royalty against the price-setter captures none of that compounding value. That's a clean distinction and I'll grant the half of it that's true: a pure spot payment for a static dataset does exactly what he says — it folds the asset into capital and walks the labeler off with cab fare. Where it breaks is the premise that labeling is a one-time consumed input.

It isn't. A deployed model that keeps earning needs reinforcement data, drift correction, red-team examples, and continuous fine-tuning — the input is a recurring dependency, not a purchase. And a recurring input priced against deployed usage is, by construction, a claim that rises with the model's earnings.

That's not theory: Reddit licensed its data to Google on ongoing terms, not a one-time sale; Shutterstock pays contributors from a recurring royalty pool tied to how its data gets used. High-value data already commands a stream, not a spot price.
